_about: The /pathway page. Step values, evidence levels, findings and proposed actions. Numbers from brain notes/2026-11-14-0145-silta-deep-data-analysis.md, sources/2026-11-14-cancerregistry-screening-by-language.md, sources/2026-11-14-europepmc-unmet-need-and-access-by-origin.md, sources/2026-11-14-espoo-equity-talk-kuitunen.md. Levels: lang = measured by native language, ind = indirect (county, origin or all invitees), none = not measured. `charts` on a step lists chart modules from app/charts/ shown in that step's detail panel.

page.title: The gap opens at the door
page.lede: People whose native language is not Finnish, Swedish or Sámi get the same screening letter but attend about 20 points less often. After they attend, most of the gap closes. Most later steps are not reported by language at all. Select a step to see the evidence and what we propose.
notes: “Other native language” includes people whose native language is unknown. The registry does not split attendance by individual language.

Language, education and region of birth overlap. Across ~290 municipalities, language still predicts lower breast and colorectal attendance after controlling for education, age, urbanisation and unemployment; for cervical screening, unemployment explains the area differences. This is an area-level model and does not prove cause.
County waiting times were read from Cancer Registry charts (±0.1 month).

Sources: Finnish Cancer Registry mass-screening statistics, published 20 May 2026 (native language, region of birth, education, previous result, delays); National Cancer Strategy 2026–2035; THL Maamu 2010–12 and FinMonik 2018–19 surveys; Norway RCT; YouScreen (London); Community Guide. Captured sources and analysis: team knowledge base (madviking/junction2026, sources/ and notes/).
page.step0: Coming later, step 0: before the letter. How people find Silta before any invitation or symptom, through community groups, migration and health services, and answers from AI assistants. It will sit in front of both routes.

big: of 1,000 Finnish, Swedish or Sámi invitees attend

s1.title: Symptom onset is recorded only in research
s1.finding: Routine registers do not record when people notice a symptom, for any group. One Finnish lymphoma study asked patients for the date, and counted every later step in days from it. One lymphoma study (DLBCL, 160 patients, 2014–2020), grouped by where patients first sought care, not by language. Lung cancer has no screening programme, so this is its only route.
s1.silta: “I noticed something”: official guidance from public Finnish health sites, in the person's language, with a link to the source. It does not diagnose or rate urgency.
county: Record the date of symptom onset at the first contact.
s1.src: Kuitunen et al., Cancer Medicine 2026;15:e71920 (Espoo talk, 13.11.2026); National Cancer Strategy 2026–2035, sub-goal 2.5.

s2.solo: Register (8 counties) and surveys, any care
s2.title: The first contact is moving to Finnish-language chat, and it reaches fewer of them
big: of residents have a native language other than Finnish or Swedish
s2.finding: Counties now route first contact through chat-based digital clinics: a nurse chat in Finnish, usually starting with a symptom checker that writes a summary for the nurse. In the eight counties studied (2022–2025), people whose native language is not Finnish or Swedish made 0.12 digital-clinic contacts per person against 0.20 overall. They were also under-represented in traditional primary care (4.1% of its users). Surveys point the same way: unmet need for a doctor's care was 5.5% among Somali-origin, 15.2% Russian-origin and 28.8% Kurdish-origin adults against 1.5% overall (THL Maamu 2010–12), and people born in Africa and the Middle East have about a third of the odds of being satisfied with access to care (FinMonik 2018–19). In a lymphoma study, people who started in public primary care made first contact on day 72, against day 42 for private or occupational care (DLBCL, 160 patients, 2014–2020, grouped by where patients first sought care, not by language).
s2.why: All of this is about any care, not cancer. The register study is descriptive (no significance tests) and does not include Helsinki or Vantaa–Kerava, the most multilingual areas. Survey figures are by origin, ages 18–64. The study cites language skills and lack of strong e-identification as barriers to digital care.
s2.silta: No login and no bank ID. The person describes what they noticed in their own language and Silta writes the Finnish summary the clinic nurse already works from. It also gives who to contact in the region, a Finnish call script to read aloud, and the right to a free interpreter.
county: Record native language and interpreter need at first contact.
Accept the Silta summary as an entry into the county's digital clinic.
s2.measure: Digital-clinic contacts per person among non-native speakers, from 0.12 towards 0.20, in the THL primary-care register linked to Statistics Finland language data (method and R code published with the study).
s2.src: Kujansivu et al., Scand J Prim Health Care 2026, doi:10.1080/02813432.2026.2686721; IJERPH 2021 18(5):2229 (Maamu); Kuusio et al., BMC Health Serv Res 2022 (FinMonik); Kuitunen et al., Cancer Medicine 2026;15:e71920 (Espoo talk, 13.11.2026).

s3.title: The first doctor visit comes 51 days later in public primary care
s3.finding: In private or occupational care the doctor visit follows first contact within a day; in public primary care it takes about three more weeks. One lymphoma study (DLBCL, 160 patients, 2014–2020), grouped by where patients first sought care, not by language. In Maamu, 95% of Somali-origin women had their latest doctor visit at a municipal health centre, against about 20% of the general population.
s3.silta: Flash cards to show symptoms, and a prepared Finnish summary for the doctor.
county: Offer the Silta summary as an input to the visit.
s3.src: Kuitunen et al., Cancer Medicine 2026;15:e71920 (Espoo talk, 13.11.2026); IJERPH 2021 18(5):2229 (Maamu).
big: days to physician visit, public primary care

s4.title: Referral comes 70 days later from public primary care
s4.finding: The gap keeps growing after referral: specialist visit on day 204 vs 118, treatment on day 207 vs 123, 84 days apart. One lymphoma study (DLBCL, 160 patients, 2014–2020), grouped by where patients first sought care, not by language. A symptom-to-biopsy time over 7 weeks was linked to worse progression-free survival (Tokola et al. 2025).
s4.silta: After-visit step: what happens next and when to call.
county: Add native language to referral and diagnosis timing.
s4.measure: Days from symptom onset to referral, by first-contact provider: one study only. Not collected routinely or by language.
s4.src: Kuitunen et al., Cancer Medicine 2026;15:e71920 (Espoo talk, 13.11.2026); Tokola et al., Cancer Medicine 2025;14(22).
